common_name: Golden Delicious Apple (Self-Fertile West Virginia Heirloom Parent of Countless Modern Apples)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Golden Delicious needs roughly 600-700 chill hours and is one of the few self-fertile apple varieties, though it still benefits from and helps pollinate compatible nearby cultivars such as Gala, Fuji, or Jonagold.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; unlike most apple varieties, Golden Delicious is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator, though its long, generous bloom period makes it one of the most valuable universal pollinizers for other apple cultivars planted nearby. Discovered as a chance seedling on the Mullins family farm in Clay County, West Virginia in the 1890s, likely a cross involving Grimes Golden, it was introduced commercially by Stark Bro's Nursery in 1914 and went on to become one of the single most important parent varieties in modern apple breeding, contributing to Gala, Jonagold, Mutsu, Pinova, Elstar, Spigold, Rubinette, Opal, and Ambrosia, among many others. The medium to large fruit ripens from green to a smooth golden yellow with light russeting around the stem, and the crisp, juicy flesh carries a mellow, honeyed sweetness with little tartness, excellent fresh, in salads, sauces, and baking. The thin skin bruises easily and the fruit softens faster in storage than firmer modern varieties, so handle gently and use within a few months of harvest; ripens midseason, typically in September.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

common_name: EverCrisp Apple (Honeycrisp x Fuji, Long-Storing Modern Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; EverCrisp requires a substantial chill period similar to its Fuji parent and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; EverCrisp requires a substantial chill period similar to its Fuji parent and a compatible pollinator planted nearby for good fruit set. Bred by Ohio orchardist Bill Dodd through the Midwest Apple Improvement Association from a cross of Honeycrisp and Fuji, it was selected specifically to capture Honeycrisp's famously crackling, juicy texture while solving that parent's notorious storage weaknesses and inconsistent bearing. The large, red-blushed fruit ripens later than Honeycrisp, typically in October, and keeps its crisp texture and sweet-tart flavor in cold storage for many months longer than Honeycrisp, with far less bruising and breakdown. Thin fruit clusters in early summer for larger apples, provide a compatible pollinator variety within range, and harvest once the background color shifts and fruit separates easily from the spur.

common_name: Sundowner Apple (Cripps Red, Late-Season Low-Chill Keeper Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sundowner has a comparatively low chill requirement (around 400-500 hours) similar to its sibling Cripps Pink and needs a long, warm growing season with a mild, extended autumn to ripen fully.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps at the Western Australian Department of Agriculture from the same Golden Delicious x Lady Williams cross that produced Cripps Pink (Pink Lady), Sundowner (also sold as Cripps Red) is an even later-ripening sibling selected for its deep red-purple skin and exceptionally dense, firm flesh that keeps in cold storage for many months longer than most dessert apples. The sweet-tart, crisp fruit needs a long, warm autumn to fully color and mature, making it well suited to mild-winter growing regions where standard high-chill apples struggle to ripen before frost. Its lower chill requirement and heat tolerance during fruit finishing make it one of the more workable late-season keeper apples for the Gulf Coast South. Harvest late in the season once the fruit reaches full deep red color, and store cool for outstanding long-term keeping quality.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension
